title: Predicting Depression via Social Media
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media
abstract: Major depression constitutes a serious challenge in personal and public health. Tens of millions of people each year suffer from depression and only a fraction receives adequate treatment. We explore the potential to use social media to detect and diagnose major depressive disorder in individuals. We first employ crowdsourcing to compile a set of Twitter users who report being diagnosed with clinical depression, based on a standard psychometric instrument. Through their social media postings over a year preceding the onset of depression, we measure behavioral attributes relating to social engagement, emotion, language and linguistic styles, ego network, and mentions of antidepressant medications. We leverage these behavioral cues, to build a statistical classifier that provides estimates of the risk of depression, before the reported onset. We find that social media contains useful signals for characterizing the onset of depression in individuals, as measured through decrease in social activity, raised negative affect, highly clustered egonetworks, heightened relational and medicinal concerns, and greater expression of religious involvement. We believe our findings and methods may be useful in developing tools for identifying the onset of major depression, for use by healthcare agencies; or on behalf of individuals, enabling those suffering from depression to be more proactive about their mental health.

claims.text: Social media activity contains behavioral signals capable of predicting major depressive disorder in individuals prior to reported onset.
Individuals in the depression class exhibit 38% lower post volume compared to the non-depression class.
Individuals in the depression class make 32% fewer @-replies compared to the non-depression class.
Individuals in the depression class express 28% higher negative affect in their Twitter posts compared to the non-depression class.
Individuals in the depression class express 11% lower emotional activation compared to the non-depression class.
Twitter posts from individuals in the depression class contain 68% higher usage of first-person pronouns compared to the non-depression class.
Twitter posts from individuals in the depression class contain 71% lower usage of third-person pronouns compared to the non-depression class.

An RBF Support Vector Machine classifier using dimension-reduced social media and demographic features achieves 70.35% positive class accuracy and 0.742 precision in predicting depression ahead of onset.

limitations.text: Prior depression research relies heavily on small, homogeneous samples and retrospective self-reports that lack temporal granularity.
Given limited availability of data, the authors could not confirm whether neighbors of users in the depressed class were also depressed.

future_work.text: Developing scalable social media analysis methods for automated public health tracking at population scale.
Tracking the diffusion of affective disorders, identifying crisis event trauma impacts, and modeling help-seeking behavior and suicide risk.

methodologies.name: Crowdsourced Ground Truth Labeling
methodologies.description: Collected self-reported depression diagnosis histories and psychometric scale scores via Amazon Mechanical Turk using CES-D and BDI screening tests.
datasets: Amazon Mechanical Turk crowdworker survey responses

methodologies.name: Social Media Behavioral Feature Extraction
methodologies.description: Extracted daily dynamic time-series features capturing engagement, egocentric graph metrics, LIWC affect and style, and depression topical lexicons across one year of Twitter activity.
conditions: 1 year of tweets preceding reported depression onset for positive class
1 year of tweets preceding survey date for negative class

methodologies.name: SVM Predictive Modeling
methodologies.description: Trained Support Vector Machine classifiers with an RBF kernel using 188 standardized dynamic and demographic features (including PCA dimensionality reduction) to predict MDD risk.
